finding.claim: GET /mirror fetches an attacker-supplied URL. The host check is a bare suffix match (endswith 'example.com') with no dot boundary, and the resolved IP is never checked. An attacker can register a lookalike domain such as evilexample.com, point it at an internal or link-local address (127.0.0.1, 10.x, 169.254.169.254), and the server will request it.
finding.source: mirror.py:11 - 'url: str' query parameter on GET /mirror (attacker-controlled)

trace.note: url is taken straight from the query string; no scheme, port, or IP restriction
host = urlparse(url).hostname or '' - hostname is lowercased but otherwise used as-is
host.endswith('example.com') matches 'evilexample.com' (no leading dot), so an attacker-owned lookalike domain passes
a new AsyncClient is created with no address filtering
c.get(url) requests the original string; DNS resolves at request time, so the check does not bind to the IP actually contacted (DNS rebinding also works)
only len(r.text) is returned, so this is a response-length oracle rather than a full body read-back

finding.guards_checked: (1) Hostname suffix check, line 13: bypassed by any attacker-registered domain ending in 'example.com' without a dot boundary, and by DNS resolving to a private or metadata IP because the IP is never checked. (2) Scheme: not restricted, but httpx only speaks http/https, so file:// and similar are unreachable. (3) Redirects: httpx.AsyncClient defaults to follow_redirects=False, so a redirect from an allowed host to an internal host is not followed. This holds for the default config and would break if follow_redirects=True were set. (4) Port: unrestricted. (5) Credentials in URL: urlparse().hostname takes the part after the last '@', so userinfo tricks like 'https://example.com@evil.com' fail the check; not exploitable here.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is `host.endswith("example.com")` at mirror.py:13, which has no dot boundary and is not a closing guard. `ALLOWED_SUFFIX` (mirror.py:7) is defined but never used. No IP or resolved-address check exists, and the request at mirror.py:16 uses the original URL string.
verdict.reason: The `url` query parameter (mirror.py:11) reaches `c.get(url)` (mirror.py:16) on an unauthenticated route, and the only check at mirror.py:13 is a bare `endswith("example.com")` that accepts an attacker-registered `evilexample.com` resolving to 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254; the trace matches the code, and httpx's default follow_redirects=False at mirror.py:15 does not block this direct request.

finding.claim: Possible parser differential between urllib.parse.urlparse (used for the check) and httpx's URL parser (used for the request). urlparse splits netloc only on '/', '?', and '#', so a backslash in the authority is not a delimiter. Input like 'http://evil.com\@example.com/' would then yield hostname 'example.com' for the check, while httpx may connect to 'evil.com'. Not verified: the sandbox denied running the test, and the httpx version is unknown.

trace.note: urlparse(url).hostname computes the host used for the check
endswith check runs on that host and would pass
httpx parses the same raw string independently and may choose a different host

finding.guards_checked: Host suffix check at line 13 only. No normalization, no reparse of the URL, and no check on the URL httpx actually uses.

verdict.guard_found: Only mirror.py:13, `host.endswith("example.com")`, which is a suffix check and does not close the finding. No exact hostname set check, no anchored match, and no re-check of the URL httpx actually requests.
verdict.reason: The `url` query parameter (mirror.py:11) reaches `c.get(url)` (mirror.py:16) and is gated only by the unanchored suffix test at mirror.py:13, so `http://evilexample.com/` passes the check and is fetched, which is a direct SSRF bypass without any parser differential. The candidate's specific backslash-differential mechanism (lines 12 and 16) is unproven because httpx's parser behavior cannot be checked from the readable files, but that part does not affect the verdict.
